question_text: If y = log(sec x + tan x), find dy/dx.

mark_split.label: Take sec x common and cancel

recall_prompt: Say how you would do this one — say what you differentiate first and what cancels at the end.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Apply the log chain rule
steps.margin_note: First mark. log u differentiates to (1/u)·du/dx. Both terms inside must be differentiated: sec x gives sec x tan x and tan x gives sec²x.
steps.memory_tip: The bracket inside the log becomes the denominator, written out unchanged; its derivative is what goes on top.
lines: y = log(sec x + tan x),  where log is the natural logarithm.
Here sec x + tan x > 0, so cos x > 0.
For u = sec x + tan x,  d/dx(log u) = (1/u) · du/dx
du/dx = d/dx(sec x) + d/dx(tan x) = sec x tan x + sec²x
∴ dy/dx = (sec x tan x + sec²x)/(sec x + tan x)

recall.must_convey: That d/dx(log u) = (1/u)·du/dx, with du/dx = sec x tan x + sec²x over the denominator sec x + tan x.
accept: log u differentiates to one over u times du by dx
the bracket goes to the denominator and its derivative goes on top
sec x gives sec x tan x and tan x gives sec squared x
log lo unna bracket kinda vasthundi, daani derivative paina
one by sec x plus tan x times the derivative of the bracket

steps.why: Both derivatives inside the bracket are standard results, so this line is fully earned by quoting them correctly. Writing the fraction before simplifying also protects the mark if the cancelling is then missed.
common_mistakes: Writing d/dx(sec x) = sec²x, confusing it with the derivative of tan x.
Differentiating the denominator as well, as though it were a quotient.

steps.label: Take sec x common and cancel
steps.margin_note: Second mark. sec x is a common factor of both numerator terms. Once it is taken out, the bracket that remains is exactly the denominator, so it cancels.
steps.memory_tip: This is a standard result worth knowing on sight: log(sec x + tan x) differentiates to sec x, with nothing left over.
lines: Take sec x common in the numerator:
sec x tan x + sec²x = sec x(tan x + sec x)
∴ dy/dx = sec x(sec x + tan x)/(sec x + tan x)

recall.must_convey: That sec x is taken common, the bracket cancels with the denominator, and dy/dx = sec x.
accept: take sec x common and the bracket cancels
numerator becomes sec x into sec x plus tan x so it cancels
sec x common teeste bracket cancel avuthundi
everything cancels and only sec x is left

steps.why: The cancelling is what makes this a two-mark question rather than a messy one. An answer left as the unsimplified fraction is not wrong, but the examiner is looking for the clean sec x.
common_mistakes: Stopping at the unsimplified fraction and not taking sec x common.
Cancelling sec x with sec x in the denominator instead of cancelling the whole bracket.

insider_note: The numerator factorises as sec x(sec x + tan x), which cancels the whole denominator. The answer is just sec x — a surprisingly clean result that is easy to distrust.
